title: Daily life, and the letter بـ
goal: Describe your daily routine — and master one little letter that brings every Egyptian verb to life: the prefix بـ.
bekal: form present-tense verbs for all eight persons
tell the form with بـ from the form without بـ
describe your day from getting up to going to bed

dialogs.title: حوار — يوم عادي
dialogs.intro: In class, the teacher asks each student to describe their day. It's Budi's turn, and Ustaz Sameh interrupts with questions.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.text: يلا يا بودي، احكيلنا. بتعمل إيه كل يوم؟
lines.baca: yalla ya Buudi, ihkiilna. bti‘mil ’ēh kull yōm?
lines.id: Come on, Budi, tell us. What do you do every day?
lines.literal: come-on O Budi, tell-us. you-do what every day?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.baca: baṣha s-saa‘a sitta, wi baṣalli l-fagr.
lines.id: I get up at six and pray the dawn prayer.
lines.literal: I-wake-up the-hour six, and I-pray the-dawn.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.id: And then? What do you have for breakfast?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: بفطر فول وعيش. بحب الفول أوي.
lines.id: I have ful and bread. I really love ful.
lines.literal: I-breakfast ful and bread. I-love the-ful very.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.text: ما شاء الله، بقيت مصري! وبتيجي المعهد إزاي؟
lines.baca: ma sha’allaah, ba’ēt maṣri! wi bitiigi l-ma‘had izzaay?
lines.id: Mashallah, you've become Egyptian! And how do you get to the institute?
lines.literal: what-God-willed, you-became Egyptian! and you-come the-institute how?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: بركب المترو، وبعدين بمشي عشر دقايق.
lines.baca: barkab il-mitro, wi ba‘dēn bamshi ‘ashar da’aayi’.
lines.id: I take the metro, and then I walk ten minutes.
lines.literal: I-ride the-metro, and then I-walk ten minutes.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.id: And where do you eat at lunchtime?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: بعض الأيام باكل بره، وأيام باكل في البيت.
lines.baca: ba‘ḍ il-ayyaam baakul barra, wi ayyaam baakul fil-bēt.
lines.id: Some days I eat out, other days I eat at home.
lines.literal: some the-days I-eat outside, and days I-eat in the-house.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.id: And what do you do in the evening?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: بذاكر شوية، وبكلم عيلتي، وبنام بدري.
lines.baca: bazaakir shuwayya, wi bakallim ‘elti, wi banaam badri.
lines.id: I study a bit, call my family, and go to bed early.
lines.literal: I-study a-little, and I-call my-family, and I-sleep early.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: حوالي عشرة. بس النهاردة عايز أسهر شوية.
lines.id: Around ten. But today I want to stay up a bit.
lines.literal: around ten. but today want I-stay-up a-little.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: منى بتعزمنا على العشا في بيتهم.
lines.id: Mona's invited us to dinner at her family's house.
lines.literal: Mona she-invites-us on the-dinner in their-house.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.text: بالهنا والشفا! ده أحسن درس عربي.
lines.id: Enjoy! That's the best Arabic lesson there is.
lines.literal: with-the-joy and-the-healing! this best lesson Arabic.

notes: **The prefix بـ marks an action that actually happens** — either as a daily routine or right now. Egyptian doesn't distinguish the two, so بشرب شاي can mean "I drink tea (every day)" or "I'm drinking tea". Context decides: where English needs two forms, Egyptian uses one.

**Without بـ, a verb isn't a sentence yet.** The form أشرب on its own means nothing — it's waiting for a word like عايز، لازم، ممكن in front of it. Hold on tight to this division of labor from now on.
**The prefix بـ attaches in front of the person prefix; it doesn't replace it.** So أشرب becomes بشرب, and يشرب becomes بيشرب. For "I", the أ prefix melts away completely: بشرب, not بأشرب.

**The word بقى here isn't the sentence-ending nudge but a verb.** بقيت مصري means "you've become Egyptian". The same word doing two different jobs happens a lot in Egyptian and never confuses its speakers.

**The word يعني is the most frequently spoken word in Egypt.** It means "it means" or "that is", but it's also used as a filler, like "I mean" or "like" in English. If you hear an Egyptian talk for a minute without one يعني, they're reading from a script.

**The phrase بالهنا والشفا is said to someone about to eat.** Literally "with enjoyment and good health". The reply is الله يهنيك. It's used much more loosely than you'd expect — including to someone who's just holding a glass of tea.

grammars.title: Present-tense verbs, all eight persons
body: Egyptian marks the subject at the **front** of the verb, not with a separate word as English does. The prefixes are the same for every verb; only the body of the word changes.
after: Notice that **انت and هي use the same prefix**: بتشرب means both "you drink" and "she drinks". Sentences are never ambiguous, because the pronoun is usually said or the context is clear.
For a woman you're talking to and for the plural, there's an extra piece at the **end**: ـي for انتي, and ـوا for انتوا and هما. So the verb gets squeezed from both sides.
The pronouns أنا، انت، هو are optional. بشرب شاي is already a complete sentence; adding أنا just adds emphasis. English always needs the "I", so get used to dropping it.

grammars.title: Verbs you can't predict, and how to tame them
body: The vowel in the middle of an Egyptian verb can't be worked out from the past tense. It has to be learned as a pair: past and present together.
after: The rows just before ذاكر are **hollow verbs** (with a weak middle letter) — راح، جه، قال، نام. Their past tense shortens for some persons: رحت *ruht* (I went), not راحت. Details in unit 14.

What you need to do now isn't memorize how they're formed but memorize the **pairs** — just as learners of English memorize go and went. A list of the forty most common verbs is at the back of the book.

sections.title: A day from waking up to going to sleep

blocks.text: To string a day together, you only need three linking words: الأول *il-awwil* (first), بعدين *ba‘dēn* (then), وفي الآخر *wi fil-aakhir* (and finally). With the verbs above and these three links, you can already talk for a full minute without stopping.

blocks.title: Time words that attach to a sentence
items: Parts of the day: الصبح *is-ṣubh* (morning), الضهر *id-ḍuhr* (noon), العصر *il-‘aṣr* (afternoon), بالليل *bil-lēl* (at night).
How often: كل يوم (every day), دايماً *daayman* (always), عادةً *‘aadatan* (usually), أحياناً *ahyaanan* (sometimes), أبداً *abadan* (never).
The word أبداً always goes with a negative sentence: مابشربش قهوة أبداً (I never drink coffee). On its own it means nothing.

blocks.text: All the following sentences use the بـ form, and all of them put the question word at the end. Swap the verb, and you have dozens of new questions.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: what are you doing? what do you do?
what time do you get up?

blocks.text: Look at the first one. The question بتعمل إيه؟ is one of the most flexible in Egyptian: it can mean "what do you do?", "what are you up to?", or "what are you going to do?" — depending on tone and situation. If you can only memorize one question from this unit, make it this one.

items: I get up at six every day.
Where do you work? (to a woman)
He takes the metro to the university.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of the verb.
Answer these questions about yourself with one Egyptian sentence each.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: بصحى الساعة ستة كل يوم. — بتشتغلي فين؟ — بيركب المترو للجامعة. — بنتغدى في البيت. — بيتفرجوا على التليفزيون بالليل.
بصحى الساعة ستة. — بفطر عيش وجبنة. — بشتغل في شركة. — بركب المترو. — بذاكر بالليل.
بصحى الساعة ستة كل يوم. — بركب المترو وبعدين بمشي. — بتعمل إيه كل يوم؟ — أحياناً باكل في البيت. — بذاكر شوية بالليل.
wave: Before you go to bed tonight, describe your own day out loud in six sentences starting with بـ. Use الأول and بعدين to link them.
